result.summary: Pindar's ode celebrates Phylakidas of Aigina, victor at the Isthmian games, and his brother Pytheas, who trained him. It praises wealth, fame and the heroes of Aiakos' line, recalls Aigina's seamen at Salamis, and ends by calling for a crown for Pytheas.

scenes.title: Hymn to Theia and fame

scenes.title: Salamis and the victors
scenes.summary: Aigina's seamen saved Salamis; Pindar praises the family and calls for a crown for Pytheas.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar's maxim urging mortals to accept human limits.
Succinct statement that human success depends on the gods.

analysis.text: The ode links success, wealth and fame, and says poetry preserves glory while mortals must stay within human limits.
Written soon after Salamis (about 478 B.C.), it praises Aigina's part in the Persian War, linking athletic victory to heroic past.

language_notes.text: Euruphaessa means 'wide-shining'; the second name is a transliteration of a Greek word for 'golden', which the editor links to gold and wealth.
'Prize gold as mighty above all things' means men value gold most because Theia's power gives it and the glory it brings its worth.
'Seek not to be as Zeus' warns against aspiring to godhood; success and fame already make a mortal's portion complete.
A pankratiast competed in the pankration, a brutal combination of wrestling and boxing. Isthmos is the Isthmus of Corinth, site of the Isthmian Games.
The sons of Aiakos are the Aiginetan heroes, such as Peleus and Telamon, descended from Aiakos, legendary king of Aigina; Pindar often celebrates them.
'She' is probably the poet's Muse or the ode's subject, the glory of the family; the pronoun is ambiguous. 'Grudge not' addresses the audience or singers.
'Cunning in words' means skilled poets, who find material for their songs in the heroes' deeds, granted by Zeus.
Oinone is the old name of Aigina. The two sackings of Troy: first with Herakles against Laomedon, later in the Trojan War with the sons of Atreus.
"Drive me upward" asks the Muse to lift the poet's song to higher themes; the questions are rhetorical, answered by the Aiakidai in sentence 18.
"Even they" answers the questions: the slayers were the Aiakidai, whose home is Aigina. "Proclaimeth" is archaic for proclaims.
Refers to the battle of Salamis (480 BC), where Aiginetan ships fought the Persians; "Aias' city" recalls Aias (Ajax), an Aiakid hero of Salamis.
The fillet is a woolen headband tied on victors, often with a garland, as a mark of honour.

context_notes.text: The battle of Salamis (480 B.C.) was a Greek naval victory over Persia, in which Aigina's fleet fought notably.
The Graces were goddesses of charm and beauty who accompanied poetry and song. Aigina is described as governed by fair, equal laws.
Pindar lists local heroes honoured with cult sacrifice: the sons of Oineus (including Meleager and Tydeus), Iolaos of Thebes, Perseus of Argos, and the Spartan twins Polydeukes and Kastor.
Kyknos, Hektor and Memnon were great warriors slain by Herakles, Achilles and Achilles respectively; Achilles was a grandson of Aiakos.
Pytheas was Phylakidas' trainer and uncle; Phylakidas won in the pancratium or wrestling event at the Isthmian games.

literary_notes.text: Pindar directly addresses the goddess Theia, opening the hymn and crediting her with giving gold and victory their value.
Life's 'bloom' and the 'flowers of wealth' compare a prosperous life to a garden at its sweetest.
This compact proverb states the poem's moral of mortal limits, a typical Pindaric gnomic statement.
The poem's recurring theme that poetry preserves glory appears here: songs make heroes' fame last through immeasurable time.
Aigina is called a tower that tempts valour to climb, picturing the island's glory as a height heroes strive to reach.
Pindar's tongue holds many arrows, picturing his praise as a quiver of weapons, and the battle is a storm of hail-like death.
Pindar stresses that Zeus alone governs outcomes, reminding the reader that human triumph depends on the gods.
Pindar addresses an unnamed attendant or Muse with commands, giving the close a ritual, celebratory tone.
